entries.4fd4a5ea2f3607578ee8e7f73f203480981aca22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv103"/><title type="x-ms">Zephaniah</title> <div sID="gen20643" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20644" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">This</hi> prophet is placed last, as he was last in time, of all the minor prophets before the captivity, and not long before Jeremiah, who lived at the time of the captivity. He foretels the general destruction of Judah and Jerusalem by the Chaldeans, and sets their sins in order before them, which had provoked God to bring their ruin upon them, calls them to repentance, threatens the neighbouring nations with the like destructions, and gives encouraging promises of their joyful return out of captivity in due time, which have a reference to the grace of the gospel. We have, in the <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.1">first verse</reference>, an account of the prophet and the date of his prophecy, which supersedes our enquiry concerning them here. <div eID="gen20644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20645" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20646" type="x-p"/> After the title of the book (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.1">ver. 1</reference>) here is, I. A threatening of the destruction of Judah and Jerusalem, an utter destruction, by the Chaldeans, <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.2-Zeph.1.4">ver. 2-4</reference>. II. A charge against them for their gross sin, which provoked God to bring that destruction upon them (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.5-Zeph.1.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>); and so he goes on in the rest of the chapter, setting both the judgments before them, that they might prevent them or prepare for them, and the sins that destroy them, that they might judge themselves, and justify God in what was brought upon them. 1. They must hold their peace because they had greatly sinned, <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.7-Zeph.1.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. But, 2, They shall howl because the trouble will be great. The day of the Lord is near, and it will be a terrible day, <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.10-Zeph.1.18">ver. 10-18</reference>. Such fair and timely warning as this did God give to the Jews of the approaching captivity; but they hardened their neck, which made their destruction remediless. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv103"/> <div eID="gen20646" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20645" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgment Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 612.)</title> <div sID="gen20647" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> which came unto Zephaniah the son of Cushi, the son of Gedaliah, the son of Amariah, the son of Hizkiah, in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah. <hi type="super">2</hi> I will utterly consume all <hi type="italic">things</hi> from off the land, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">3</hi> I will consume man and beast; I will consume the fowls of the heaven, and the fishes of the sea, and the stumbling-blocks with the wicked; and I will cut off man from off the land, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">4</hi> I will also stretch out mine hand upon Judah, and upon all the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and I will cut off the remnant of Baal from this place, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the name of the Chemarims with the priests; <hi type="super">5</hi> And them that worship the host of heaven upon the housetops; and them that worship <hi type="italic">and</hi> that swear by the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and that swear by Malcham; <hi type="super">6</hi> And them that are turned back from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and <hi type="italic">those</hi> that have not sought the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , nor enquired for him. <div eID="gen20647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20648" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The title-page of this book (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.1">v. 1</reference>), in which we observe, 1. What authority it has, and who gave it that authority; it is from heaven, and not of men: It is <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord.</hi> 2. Who was the instrument of conveying it to the church. His name was Zephaniah, which signifies the <hi type="italic">servant of the Lord,</hi> for God <hi type="italic">revealed his secrets to his servants the prophets.</hi> The pedigree of other prophets, whose extraction we have an account of, goes no further back than their father, except Zecharias, whose grandfather also is named. But this of Zephaniah goes back four generations, and the highest mentioned is <hi type="italic">Hizkiah;</hi> it is the very same name in the original with that of Hezekiah king of Judah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.1">2 Kings xviii. 1</reference>), and refers probably to him; if so, our prophet, being lineally descended from that pious prince, and being of the royal family, could with the better grace reprove the folly of the king's children as he does, <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.8">v. 8</reference>. 3. When this prophet prophesied—<hi type="italic">in the days of Josiah king of Judah,</hi> who reigned well, and in the twelfth year of his reign began vigorously, and carried on a work of reformation, in which he destroyed idols and idolatry. Now it does not appear whether Zephaniah prophesied in the beginning of his reign; if so, we may suppose his prophesying had a great and good influence on that reformation. When he, as God's messenger, reproved the idolatries of Jerusalem, Josiah, as God's vice-gerent, removed them; and reformation is likely to go on and prosper when both magistrates and ministers do their part towards it. If it were towards the latter end of his reign that he prophesied, we sadly see how a corrupt people relapse into their former distempers. The idolatries Josiah had abolished, it should seem, returned in his own time, when the heat of the reformation began a little to abate and wear off. What good can the best reformers do with a people that hate to be reformed, as if they longed to be ruined? <div eID="gen20648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20649" type="x-p"/> II. The summary, or contents, of this book. The general proposition contained in it is, That utter destruction is coming apace upon Judah and Jerusalem for sin. Without preamble, or apology, he begins abruptly (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">By taking away I will make an end of all things from off the face of the land, Saith the Lord.</hi> Ruin is coming, utter ruin, destruction from the Almighty. He has said it who can, and will, make good what he has said: "<hi type="italic">I will utterly consume all things.</hi> I will <hi type="italic">gather</hi> all things" (so some); "I will recall all the blessings I have bestowed, because they have abused them and so forfeited them." The consumption determined shall take away, 1. The inferior creatures: <hi type="italic">I will consume the beasts, the fowls of the heaven, and the fishes of the sea</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.3">v. 3</reference>), as, in the deluge, <hi type="italic">every living substance was destroyed that was upon the face of the ground,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.7.23">Gen. vii. 23</reference>. The creatures were made for man's use, and therefore when he has perverted the use of them, and made them <hi type="italic">subject to vanity,</hi> God, to show the greatness of his displeasure against the sin of man, involves them in his punishment. The expressions are figurative, denoting universal desolation. Those that fly ever so high, as the fowls of heaven, and think themselves out of the reach of the enemies' hand—those that hide ever so close, as the fishes of the sea, and think themselves out of the reach of the enemies' eye—shall yet become a prey to them, and be utterly consumed. 2. The children of men: "<hi type="italic">I will consume man; I will cut off man from the land.</hi> The land shall be dispeopled and left uninhabited; I will destroy, not only Israel, but <hi type="italic">man.</hi> The land shall enjoy her sabbaths. I will cut off, not only the wicked men, but all men; even the few among them that are good shall be involved in this common calamity. Though they shall not be cut off from the Lord, yet they shall be <hi type="italic">cut off from the land.</hi>" It is with Judah and Jerusalem that God has this quarrel, both city and country, and upon them he will <hi type="italic">stretch out his hand,</hi> the hand of his power, the hand of his wrath; and <hi type="italic">who knows the power of his anger?</hi> <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.4">v. 4</reference>. Those that will not humble themselves under God's mighty hand shall be humbled and brought down by it. Note, Even Judah, where God is known, and Jerusalem, where his dwelling-place is, if they revolt from him and rebel against him, shall have his hand stretched out against them. 3. All wicked people, and all those things that are the matter of their wickedness (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will consume the stumbling-blocks with the wicked,</hi> the idols with the idolaters, the offences with the offenders." Josiah had taken away the stumbling-blocks, and, as far as he could, had purged the land of the monuments of idolatry, hoping that there would be no more idolatry; but <hi type="italic">the wicked will do wickedly,</hi> the dog will return to his vomit, and therefore, since the sin will not otherwise be cured, the sinners must themselves be consumed, even the <hi type="italic">wicked with the stumbling-blocks</hi> of their iniquity, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.3">Ezek. xiv. 3</reference>. Since it was not done by the sword of justice, it shall be done by the sword of war. See who the sinners are that shall be consumed. (1.) The professed idolaters, who avowed idolatry, and were wedded to it. The <hi type="italic">remnant of Baal</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">cut off,</hi> the images of Baal, and the worshippers of those images. Josiah cut off a great deal of Baal; but that which was so close as to escape the eye, or so bold as to escape the hand, of his justice, God will cut off, even all the remains of it. The Chaldeans would spare none of the images of Baal, or the worshippers of those images. The <hi type="italic">Chemarim</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">cut off;</hi> we read of them in the history of Josiah's reformation. <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.5">2 Kings xxiii. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">He put down the idolatrous priests:</hi> the word is the <hi type="italic">Chemarim.</hi> The word signifies <hi type="italic">black men,</hi> some think because they wore black clothes, affecting to appear grave, others because their faces were black with attending the altars, or the fires in which they burnt their children to Moloch. They seem to have been immediate attendants upon the service of Baal. They shall be <hi type="italic">cut off with the priests,</hi> the regulars with the seculars. The very name of them shall be cut off; the order shall be quite abolished, so as to be forgotten, or remembered with detestation. And, among other idolaters, the <hi type="italic">worshippers of the host of heaven upon the house-tops</hi> shall be cut off (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.5">v. 5</reference>), who justified themselves in their idolatry with those that did not worship images, the work of their own hands, but offered their sacrifices and burnt their incense to the sun, moon, and stars, immediately upon the tops of their houses. But God will let them know that he is a jealous God, and will not endure any rival; and, though some have thought that the most specious and plausible idolatry, yet it will appear as great an offence to God to give divine honours to a star as to give them to a stone or a stock. Even the worshippers of the host of heaven shall be consumed as well as the worshippers of the beasts of the earth or the fiends of hell. The sin of the adulteress is not the less sinful for the gaiety of the adulterer. (2.) Those also shall be consumed that think to compound the matter between God and idols, and keep an even hand between them, that halt between God and Baal, and worship between Jehovah and Moloch, and <hi type="italic">swear by both;</hi> or, as it might better be read, swear <hi type="italic">to the Lord and to Malcham.</hi> They bind themselves by oath and covenant to the service both of God and idols. They have a good opinion of the worship of the God of Israel; it is the religion of their country, and has been long so, and therefore they will by no means quit it; but they think it will be very much improved and beautified if they join with it the worship of Moloch, for that also is much used in other countries, and travellers admire it; there is a great deal of good fancy and strong flame in it. They cannot keep always to the worship of a God whom they have no visible representation of, and therefore they must have an image; and what better than the image of <hi type="italic">Moloch—a king?</hi> They think they shall effectually atone for their sin if they <hi type="italic">swear to Moloch,</hi> and, pursuant to that oath, burn their children in sacrifice to that idol; and yet, if they do amiss in that, they hope to atone for it in worshipping the God of Israel too. Note, Those that think to divide their affections and adorations between God and idols will not only come short of acceptance with God, but will have their doom with the worst of idolaters; for what communion can there be between light and darkness, Christ and Belial, God and mammon? She whose own the child is not pleads for the dividing of it, for, if Satan have half, he will have all; but the true mother says, <hi type="italic">Divide it not,</hi> for, if God have but half, he will have none. Such waters will not be long sweet, if they come from a fountain that sends forth bitter water too; what have those to do to swear by the Lord that swear by Malcham? (3.) Those also shall be consumed that have apostatized from God, together with those that never gave up their names to him, <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.6">v. 6</reference>. I will cut off, [1.] Those <hi type="italic">that are turned back from the Lord,</hi> that were well taught, and began well, that had given up their names to him, and set out at first in the worship of him, but have flown off, and turned aside, and fallen in with idolaters, and deserted those good ways of God which they were brought up in, and despised them. Those God will be sure to reckon with who are renegadoes from his service, who began in the Spirit and ended in the flesh; they shall be treated as deserters, to whom no mercy is shown. [2.] Those that <hi type="italic">have not sought the Lord,</hi> nor ever <hi type="italic">enquired for him,</hi> never made any profession of religion, and think to excuse themselves with that, shall find that this will not excuse them; nay, this is the thing laid to their charge; they are atheistical careless people, that <hi type="italic">live without God in the world;</hi> and those that do so are certainly unworthy to live upon God in the world.
entries.ada2958005a4941c0174067033a7710a140285ab: <div eID="gen20649" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgment Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 612.)</title> <div sID="gen20650" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Hold thy peace at the presence of the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> : for the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> at hand: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath prepared a sacrifice, he hath bid his guests. <hi type="super">8</hi> And it shall come to pass in the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's sacrifice, that I will punish the princes, and the king's children, and all such as are clothed with strange apparel. <hi type="super">9</hi> In the same day also will I punish all those that leap on the threshold, which fill their masters' houses with violence and deceit. <hi type="super">10</hi> And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">that there shall be</hi> the noise of a cry from the fish gate, and an howling from the second, and a great crashing from the hills. <hi type="super">11</hi> Howl, ye inhabitants of Maktesh, for all the merchant people are cut down; all they that bear silver are cut off. <hi type="super">12</hi> And it shall come to pass at that time, <hi type="italic">that</hi> I will search Jerusalem with candles, and punish the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will not do good, neither will he do evil. <hi type="super">13</hi> Therefore their goods shall become a booty, and their houses a desolation: they shall also build houses, but not inhabit <hi type="italic">them;</hi> and they shall plant vineyards, but not drink the wine thereof. <div eID="gen20650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20651" type="x-p"/> Notice is here given to Judah and Jerusalem that God is coming forth against them, and will be with them shortly; his <hi type="italic">presence,</hi> as a just avenger, <hi type="italic">his day,</hi> the day of his judgment and his wrath, are not far off, <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.7">v. 7</reference>. Those that improve not the presence of God with them as a Father, but sin away that presence, may expect his presence with them as a Judge, to call them to an account for the contempt put upon his grace. The <hi type="italic">day of the Lord</hi> will come. Men have their day now, when they take a liberty to do what they please; but <hi type="italic">God's day is at hand;</hi> it is here called his <hi type="italic">sacrifice,</hi> a sacrifice of his preparing, for the punishing of presumptuous sinners is a sacrifice to the justice of God, some reparation to his injured honour. Those that brought their offerings to other gods were themselves justly made victims to the true God. On a day of sacrifice great slaughter was made; so shall there be in Jerusalem; men shall be killed up as fast as lambs for the altar, with as little regret, with as much pleasure: <hi type="italic">The slain of the Lord shall be many.</hi> On a day of sacrifice great feasts were made upon the sacrifices; so the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem shall be feasted upon by their enemies the Chaldeans; these are the guests God has prepared and invited to come and glut themselves—their revenge with slaughter and their covetousness with plunder. Now observe, <div eID="gen20651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20652" type="x-p"/> I. Who those are that are marked to be sacrificed, that shall be visited and punished in this day of reckoning, and what it is they shall be called to an account for. 1. The royal family, because of the dignity of their place, shall be first reckoned with for their pride, and vanity, and affectation (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will punish the princes, and the king's children,</hi> who think themselves accountable to God, and that, high as they are, he is above them. They shall be punished, and all such as, like them, are clothed <hi type="italic">with strange apparel,</hi> such as, in contempt of their own country (where, probably, it was the custom to go in a very plain dress, as became the seed of Jacob that <hi type="italic">plain man</hi>), affected to appear in the fashion of other nations and introduced their modes in apparel, studying to resemble those from whom God had appointed them, even in their clothes, industriously to distinguish themselves. <hi type="italic">The princes and the king's children</hi> scorned to wear any home-made stuffs, though God had provided them <hi type="italic">fine linen</hi> and <hi type="italic">silks</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.10">Ezek. xvi. 10</reference>), but they must send abroad to strange countries for their clothes, which would not please unless they were far-fetched and dear-bought; and even those of inferior rank affected to imitate the princes and the king's children. Pride in apparel is displeasing to God, and a symptom of the degeneracy of a people. 2. The noblemen, and their stewards and servants, come next to be reckoned with (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">In the same day will I punish those that leap on the threshold,</hi> a phrase, no doubt, well understood then, and which probably signified the invading of their neighbour's rights. Entering their houses by force and violence, and seizing their possessions, they <hi type="italic">leap on the threshold,</hi> as much as to say that the house is their own and they will keep their hold of it; and, accordingly, they make all in it their own that they can lay their hands on, and so <hi type="italic">fill their masters' houses</hi> with goods gotten <hi type="italic">by violence and deceit</hi> and with all the guilt thereby contracted. Nor shall it suffice them to say that the ill-gotten gains were not for themselves but for their masters, and that what they did was by their order; for the obligations we lie under to keep God's commandments are prior and superior to the obligations we lie under to serve the interests of any master on earth. 3. The trading people, and the rich merchants, are next called to account. Iniquity is found in their end of the town, among <hi type="italic">the inhabitants of Maktesh,</hi> a low part of Jerusalem, deep like a mortar (for so the word signifies); the <hi type="italic">goldsmiths</hi> lived there (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.32">Neh. iii. 32</reference>) and the merchants; and they are now <hi type="italic">cut down</hi> (they are broken, and have shut up their shops, and become bankrupts); nay, <hi type="italic">All those that bear silver are cut off,</hi> in the first place, by the invaders, for the sake of the silver they carry, which is so far from being a protection to them that it will expose and betray them. The conquerors aimed at the wealthy men, and carried them off first, while <hi type="italic">the poor of the land escaped.</hi> Or it may be meant of a general decay of trade, which was a preface and introduction to the general destruction of the land. It is the token of a declining state when great dealers are cut down, and great bankers are cut off and become bankrupts, who cannot fall alone, but with themselves ruin many. 4. All the secure and careless people, the sons of pleasure, that live a loose idle life, are next reckoned with (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.12">v. 12</reference>); they come from all parts of the country, to take up their quarters in the head-quarters of the kingdom, where they take private lodgings, and indulge themselves in ease and luxury; but God will find them out, and punish them: <hi type="italic">At that time I will search Jerusalem with candles,</hi> to discover them, that they may be brought out to condign punishment. This intimates that they conceal themselves, as being either ashamed of the sin or afraid of the punishment of it; when the judgments of God are abroad they hope to escape by absconding and getting out of the way, but God will <hi type="italic">search Jerusalem,</hi> as search is made for a malefactor in disguise, that is harboured by his accomplices. God's hand will <hi type="italic">find out all his enemies,</hi> wherever they lie hid, and will punish not only the secret idolaters, but the secret epicures and profane; and those are the persons that are here described, and marks are given by which they will be discovered when strict search is made for them. (1.) Their dispositions are sensual: They <hi type="italic">are settled on their lees,</hi> intoxicated with their pleasures, strengthening themselves in their wealth and wickedness; they are secure and easy, and, because they have had no changes, they fear none, as Moab, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.11">Jer. xlviii. 11</reference>. They <hi type="italic">have not been emptied from vessel to vessel.</hi> They <hi type="italic">fill themselves with wine and strong drink,</hi> and banish all thought, saying, <hi type="italic">To-morrow shall be as this day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.56.12">Isa. lvi. 12</reference>. Their being <hi type="italic">settled on their lees</hi> signifies the same with being <hi type="italic">enclosed in their own fat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.17.10">Ps. xvii. 10</reference>. (2.) Their notions are atheistical. They could not live such loose lives but that they say <hi type="italic">in their heart, The Lord will not do good, neither will he do evil;</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">He will do nothing.</hi> They deny his providential government of the world: "What good and evil there is in the world comes by the wheel of fortune, and not by the disposal of a wise and supreme director." They deny his moral government, and his dispensing rewards and punishments: "<hi type="italic">The Lord will not do good</hi> to those that serve him, nor <hi type="italic">do evil</hi> to those that rebel against him; and therefore there is nothing got by religion, nor lost by sin." This was the effect of their sensuality; if they were not drowned in sense, they could not be thus senseless, nor could they be so stupid if they had not stupefied themselves with the love of pleasure. It was also the cause of their sensuality; men would not make a god of their belly if they had not at first become so vain, so vile, in their imaginations, as to think the God that made them <hi type="italic">altogether such a one as themselves.</hi> But God will <hi type="italic">punish them; their end is destruction,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Phil. iii. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen20652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20653" type="x-p"/> II. What the destruction will be with which God will punish these sinners, and what course he will take with them. 1. He will silence them (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Hold thy peace at the presence of the Lord.</hi> He will force them to hold their peace, will strike them dumb with horror and amazement. They shall be speechless. All the excuses of their sin, and exceptions against the sentence, will be overruled, and they shall not have a word to say for themselves. 2. He will <hi type="italic">sacrifice</hi> them, for it is <hi type="italic">the day of the Lord's sacrifice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.8">v. 8</reference>); he will give them into the hands of their enemies, and glorify himself thereby. 3. He will fill both city and country with lamentation (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">In that day there shall be a noise of a cry from the fish-gate,</hi> so called because near either to the fish-ponds or to the fish-market. It belonged to the city of David (<reference osisRef="2Chr.33.14">2 Chron. xxxiii. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.3.3">Neh. iii. 3</reference>); perhaps the same with that which is called the <hi type="italic">first gate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.10">Zech. xiv. 10</reference>), and, if so, it will explain what follows here, <hi type="italic">And a howling from the second,</hi> that is, the second gate, which was next to that <hi type="italic">fish-gate.</hi> The alarm shall go round the walls of Jerusalem from gate to gate; and there shall be <hi type="italic">a great crashing from the hills,</hi> a mighty noise from the mountains round about Jerusalem, from the acclamations of the victorious invaders, or from the lamentations of the timorous invaded, or from both. The inhabitants of the city, even of the closest safest part of the city, shall <hi type="italic">howl</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.11">v. 11</reference>), so clamorous shall the grief be. 4. They shall be stripped of all they have; it shall be a prey to the enemy (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Their household goods,</hi> and <hi type="italic">shop-goods,</hi> shall <hi type="italic">become a booty,</hi> and a rich booty they shall be; <hi type="italic">their houses shall be</hi> levelled with the ground and be <hi type="italic">a desolation;</hi> those of them that have <hi type="italic">built</hi> new houses <hi type="italic">shall not inherit them,</hi> but the invaders shall get and keep possession of them. And the <hi type="italic">vineyards</hi> they have planted they shall not <hi type="italic">drink the wine of,</hi> but, instead of having it for the relief of their friends that faint among them, they shall part with it for the animating of their foes that fight against them, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.30">Deut. xxviii. 30</reference>.
entries.42aa39a91fb64998f5c7dafb1d6f19e555a66b37: <div eID="gen20653" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgment Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 612.)</title> <div sID="gen20654" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> The great day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> near, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> near, and hasteth greatly, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the voice of the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : the mighty man shall cry there bitterly. <hi type="super">15</hi> That day <hi type="italic">is</hi> a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of wasteness and desolation, a day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness, <hi type="super">16</hi> A day of the trumpet and alarm against the fenced cities, and against the high towers. <hi type="super">17</hi> And I will bring distress upon men, that they shall walk like blind men, because they have sinned against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and their blood shall be poured out as dust, and their flesh as the dung. <hi type="super">18</hi> Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them in the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's wrath; but the whole land shall be devoured by the fire of his jealousy: for he shall make even a speedy riddance of all them that dwell in the land. <div eID="gen20654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20655" type="x-p"/> Nothing could be expressed with more spirit and life, nor in words more proper to startle and awaken a secure and careless people, than the warning here given to Judah and Jerusalem of the approaching destruction by the Chaldeans. That is enough to make the sinners in Zion tremble—that it is <hi type="italic">the day of the Lord,</hi> the day in which he will manifest himself by taking vengeance on them. It is <hi type="italic">the great day of the Lord,</hi> a specimen of the day of judgment, a kind of doom's-day, as the last destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans is represented to be in our Saviour's prediction concerning it, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.27">Matt. xxiv. 27</reference>. <div eID="gen20655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20656" type="x-p"/> I. This <hi type="italic">day of the Lord</hi> is here spoken of as very near. The vision is not <hi type="italic">for a great while to come,</hi> as those imagine who <hi type="italic">put the evil day far from them.</hi> Those deceive themselves who look upon it as a thing at a distance, for <hi type="italic">it is near—it is near—it hastens greatly.</hi> The prophet gives the alarm like one that is in earnest, like one that awakens a family with the cry of <hi type="italic">Fire! fire!</hi> when it is at the next door that the danger is: "<hi type="italic">It is near! it is near!</hi> and therefore it is high time to bestir yourselves, and do what you can for your own safety before it be too late." It is madness for those to slumber whose <hi type="italic">damnation slumbers not,</hi> and to linger when it hastens. <div eID="gen20656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20657" type="x-p"/> II. It is spoken of as a very dreadful day. The very <hi type="italic">voice</hi> of this <hi type="italic">day of the Lord,</hi> the noise of it, when it is coming, shall be so terrible as to make <hi type="italic">the mighty men cry there bitterly,</hi> cry for fear as children do. <hi type="italic">It shall be a vexation</hi> to <hi type="italic">hear the report</hi> of it. In the last great day of the Lord the mighty men shall cry bitterly to rocks and mountains to shelter them; but in vain. Observe how emphatically the prophet speaks of this day approaching (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.15">v. 15</reference>): It is <hi type="italic">a day of wrath,</hi> God's wrath, wrath in perfection, wrath to the utmost. It will be a day of <hi type="italic">trouble and distress</hi> to the sinners; they shall be in pain, and shall see no ways of easing or helping themselves. The miseries of the damned are summed up (perhaps with reference to this) in the <hi type="italic">indignation and wrath of God,</hi> which are the cause, and the <hi type="italic">tribulation and anguish</hi> of the sinner's <hi type="italic">soul,</hi> which are the effect, <reference osisRef="Rom.2.8-Rom.2.9">Rom. ii. 8, 9</reference>. It will be a day of <hi type="italic">trouble and distress</hi> to the inhabitants, and a day of <hi type="italic">wasteness and desolation</hi> to the whole land; that fruitful land shall be turned into a wilderness. It shall be <hi type="italic">a day of darkness and gloominess;</hi> every thing shall look dismal, and there shall not be the least gleam of comfort, or glimpse of hope; look round, and it is all black. It is <hi type="italic">a day of clouds and thick darkness;</hi> there is not only nothing encouraging, but every thing threatening; the thick clouds are big with storms and tempests. <div eID="gen20657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20658" type="x-p"/> III. It is spoken of as a destroying day, <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.16-Zeph.1.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. It shall be destroying, 1. To places, even the strongest and best fortified: <hi type="italic">A day of the trumpet and alarm against the fenced cities,</hi> to break into them, and against the <hi type="italic">high towers,</hi> to bring them down; for what forts, what fences, can hold out against the wrath of God? 2. To persons (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will bring distress upon men,</hi> the strongest and stoutest of men; their hearts and hands shall fail them; they shall <hi type="italic">walk like blind men,</hi> wandering endlessly, <hi type="italic">because they have sinned against the Lord.</hi>" Note, Those that walk as bad men will justly be left to walk as blind men, always in the dark, in doubt and danger, without any guide or comfort, and falling at length into the ditch. Because they have <hi type="italic">sinned against the Lord</hi> he will deliver them into the hands of cruel enemies, that shall <hi type="italic">pour out their blood as dust,</hi> so profusely, and with as little regret, and <hi type="italic">their flesh</hi> shall be thrown <hi type="italic">as dung</hi> upon the dunghill. <div eID="gen20658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20659" type="x-p"/> IV. The destruction of that day will be unavoidable and universal, <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.18">v. 18</reference>. 1. There shall be no escaping it by ransom: <hi type="italic">Neither their silver nor their gold,</hi> which they have hoarded up so covetously against the evil day, or which they have spent so prodigally to make friends for such a time, <hi type="italic">shall be able to deliver them in the day of the Lord's wrath.</hi> Another prophet borrowed these words from this, with reference to the same event, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.19">Ezek. vii. 19</reference>. Note, Riches profit not in the day of wrath, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.4">Prov. xi. 4</reference>. Nay, riches expose to the wrath of men (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.13">Eccl. v. 13.</reference>), and riches abused to the wrath of God. 2. There shall be no escaping it by flight or concealment; for the <hi type="italic">whole land shall be devoured by the fire of his jealousy,</hi> and where then can a hiding-place be found? See what the fire of God's jealousy is, and what the force of it; it will devour whole lands; how then can particular persons stand before it? He shall make riddance, <hi type="italic">a speedy riddance, of all those that dwell in the land,</hi> as the husbandman, when he rids his ground, cuts up all the briers and thorns for the fire. Note, Sometimes the judgments of God make riddance, even utter riddance, with sinful nations, a speedy riddance; their destruction is effected, is completed, in a little time. Let not sinners be laid asleep by the patience of God, for when the measure of their iniquity is full his justice will both overtake and overcome, will make quick work and thorough work.  <chapter eID="Zeph.1"/> <div eID="gen20659" type="x-p"/>

entries.3cba5fc55d85809696e80a109c1e67736072237f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12922"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen24169" type="x-p"/> Zephaniah, ninth in order of the minor prophets, prophesied "in the days of Josiah" (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.1">Zep 1:1</reference>), that is, between 642 and 611 B.C. The name means "Jehovah hath guarded," literally, "hidden" (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Psa 27:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.83.3">83:3</reference>). The specification in the introductory heading, of not only his father, but also his grandfather, and great-grandfather, and great-great-grandfather, implies that the latter were persons of note, or else the design was to distinguish him from another Zephaniah of note at the time of the captivity. The Jews' supposition, that persons recorded as a prophet's ancestors were themselves endowed with the prophetic spirit, seems groundless. There is no impossibility of the Hezekiah, who was Zephaniah's great-great-grandfather, being King Hezekiah as to the number of generations; for Hezekiah's reign of twenty-nine years, and his successor's reign of fifty-five years, admit of four generations interposing between. Yet the omission of the designation, "king of Judah," is fatal to the theory (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.25.1">Pr 25:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.38.9">Is 38:9</reference>).<div eID="gen24169" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24168" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24170" type="x-p"/> He must have flourished in the earlier part of Josiah's reign. In <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.13-Zeph.2.15">Zep 2:13-15</reference> he foretells the doom of Nineveh, which happened in 625 B.C.; and in <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.4">Zep 1:4</reference> he denounces various forms of idolatry, and specially that of Baal. Now Josiah's reformation began in the twelfth and was completed in the eighteenth year of his reign. Zephaniah, therefore, in denouncing Baal worship, co-operated with that good king in his efforts, and so must have prophesied somewhere between the twelfth and eighteenth years of his reign. The silence of the historical books is no argument against this, as it would equally apply against Jeremiah's prophetical existence at the same time. Jewish tradition says that Zephaniah had for his colleagues Jeremiah, whose sphere of labor was the thoroughfares and market places, and Huldah the prophetess, who exercised her vocation in the college in Jerusalem.<div eID="gen24170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24171" type="x-p"/> The prophecy begins with the nation's sin and the fearful retribution coming at the hands of the Chaldeans. These are not mentioned by name, as in Jeremiah; for the prophecies of the latter, being nearer the fulfilment, become more explicit than those of an earlier date. The second chapter dooms the persecuting states in the neighborhood as well as Judea itself. The third chapter denounces Jerusalem, but concludes with the promise of her joyful re-establishment in the theocracy.<div eID="gen24171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24172" type="x-p"/> The style, though not generally sublime, is graphic and vivid in details (compare <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.4-Zeph.1.12">Zep 1:4-12</reference>). The language is pure, and free from Aramaisms. There are occasional coincidences with former prophets (compare <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.14">Zep 2:14</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.34.11">Is 34:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.15">Zep 2:15</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.47.8">Is 47:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.10">Zep 3:10</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1">Is 18:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.8">Zep 2:8</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Is 16:6</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.5">Zep 1:5</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Jer.8.2">Jr 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.12">Zep 1:12</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Jer.48.11">Jr 48:11</reference>). Such coincidences in part arise from the phraseology of Hebrew prophetic poetry being the common language of the inspired brotherhood. The New Testament, at <reference osisRef="Rom.15.6">Ro 15:6</reference>, seems to refer to <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.9">Zep 3:9</reference>.<div eID="gen24172" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zeph.1.1-Zeph.1.18">Zep 1:1-18</reference>. God's Severe Judgment on Judah for Its Idolatry and Neglect of Him: The Rapid Approach of the Judgment, and the Impossibility of Escape.</title> <div sID="gen24173" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12922"/><hi type="bold">1. days of Josiah--</hi>Had their idolatries been under former kings, they might have said, Our kings have forced us to this and that. But under Josiah, who did all in his power to reform them, they have no such excuse.<div eID="gen24173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24174" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">son of Amon--</hi>the idolater, whose bad practices the Jews clung to, rather than the good example of Josiah, his son; so incorrigible were they in sin.<div eID="gen24174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Judah--</hi>Israel's ten tribes had gone into captivity before this. <div eID="gen24175" type="x-p"/>
entries.40ad9e98b0f0a7939e55857b6c47091c83b421cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12923"/><div sID="gen24176" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12923"/><hi type="bold">2. utterly consume--</hi>from a root to "sweep away," or "scrape off utterly." See <reference osisRef="Jer.8.13">Jr 8:13</reference>, Margin, and here.<div eID="gen24176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from off the land--</hi>of Judah. <div eID="gen24177" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ba9efd79e891bab00cfcaf19b5178f687b8041d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12924"/><div sID="gen24178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12924"/>3. Enumeration in detail of the "all things" (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.2">Zep 1:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.9.10">Jr 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.4.3">Ho 4:3</reference>).<div eID="gen24178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24179" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the stumbling-blocks--</hi>idols which cause Judah to offend or stumble (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.3">Eze 14:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.7">4, 7</reference>).<div eID="gen24179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24180" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with the wicked--</hi>The idols and their worshippers shall be involved in a common destruction. <div eID="gen24180" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7c273749d3bc28ac1fa281313037a9268f0efc4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12925"/><div sID="gen24181" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12925"/><hi type="bold">4. stretch out mine hand--</hi>indicating some remarkable and unusual work of vengeance (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.25">Is 5:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.12">9:12</reference>, 17, 21).<div eID="gen24181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Judah--</hi>including Benjamin. These two tribes are to suffer, which thought themselves perpetually secure, because they escaped the captivity in which the ten tribes were involved.<div eID="gen24182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jerusalem--</hi>the fountainhead of the evil. God begins with His sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.6">Eze 9:6</reference>), and those who are nigh Him (<reference osisRef="Lev.10.3">Le 10:3</reference>).<div eID="gen24183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24184" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the remnant of Baal--</hi>the remains of Baal worship, which as yet Josiah was unable utterly to eradicate in remote places. Baal was the Phoenician tutelary god. From the time of the Judges (<reference osisRef="Judg.2.13">Jud 2:13</reference>), Israel had fallen into this idolatry; and Manasseh lately had set up this idol within Jehovah's temple itself (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.3">2Ki 21:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.7">5, 7</reference>). Josiah began his reformation in the twelfth year of his reign (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.4">2Ch 34:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.8">8</reference>), and in the eighteenth had as far as possible completed it.<div eID="gen24184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24185" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chemarims--</hi>idol priests, who had not reached the age of puberty; meaning "ministers of the gods" [Servius on Æneid, 11], the same name as the Tyrian Camilli, r and l being interchangeable (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.10.5">Ho 10:5</reference>, Margin). Josiah is expressly said (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.5">2Ki 23:5</reference>, Margin) to have "put down the Chemarim." The Hebrew root means "black" (from the black garments which they wore or the marks which they branded on their foreheads); or "zealous," from their idolatrous fanaticism. The very "name," as well as themselves, shall be forgotten.<div eID="gen24185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24186" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the priests--</hi>of Jehovah, of Aaronic descent, who ought to have used all their power to eradicate, but who secretly abetted, idolatry (compare <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.4">Zep 3:4</reference>; Eze 8:1-18; 22:26; 44:10). From the priests Zephaniah passes to the people. <div eID="gen24186" type="x-p"/>
entries.08c085c683407d09656ac6ddf64b6b36568669a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12926"/><div sID="gen24187" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12926"/><hi type="bold">5. worship the host of heaven--</hi>Saba: whence, in contrast to Sabeanism, Jehovah is called Lord of Sabaoth.<div eID="gen24187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24188" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon the housetops--</hi>which were flat (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.5">2Ki 23:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.12">6, 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.19.13">Jr 19:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.29">32:29</reference>).<div eID="gen24188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24189" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">swear by the Lord--</hi>rather, "swear to Jehovah" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.14">2Ch 15:14</reference>); solemnly dedicating themselves to Him (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.48.1">Is 48:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.4.15">Ho 4:15</reference>).<div eID="gen24189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24190" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>"and yet (with strange inconsistency, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.21">1Ki 18:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.39">Eze 20:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.24">Mt 6:24</reference>) swear by Malcham," that is, "their king" [Maurer]: the same as Molech (see on <reference osisRef="Amos.5.25">Am 5:25</reference>), and "Milcom the god of ... Ammon" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.33">1Ki 11:33</reference>). If Satan have half the heart, he will have all; if the Lord have but half offered to Him, He will have none. <div eID="gen24190" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c7d0f9bcc524e931388c57e89d738416c0156a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12927"/><div sID="gen24191" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12927"/>6. This verse describes more comprehensively those guilty of defection from Jehovah in any way (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.13">Jr 2:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">17</reference>). <div eID="gen24191" type="x-p"/>
entries.51921e6e9848e400198162677cdcd1ca296867ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12928"/><div sID="gen24192" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12928"/><hi type="bold">7. Hold thy peace at the presence of the Lord--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hab.2.20">Ha 2:20</reference>). Let the earth be silent at His approach [Maurer]. Or, "Thou whosoever hast been wont to speak against God, as if He had no care about earthly affairs, cease thy murmurs and self-justifications; submit thyself to God, and repent in time" [Calvin].<div eID="gen24192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24193" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord ... prepared a sacrifice--</hi>namely, a slaughter of the guilty Jews, the victims due to His justice (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.6">Is 34:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.10">Jr 46:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.17">Eze 39:17</reference>).<div eID="gen24193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24194" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bid his guests--</hi>literally, "sanctified His called ones" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.13.3">Is 13:3</reference>). It enhances the bitterness of the judgment that the heathen Chaldeans should be sanctified, or consecrated as it were, by God as His priests, and be called to eat the flesh of the elect people; as on feast days the priests used to feast among themselves on the remains of the sacrifices [Calvin]. English Version takes it not of the priests, but the guests bidden, who also had to "sanctify" or purify themselves before coming to the sacrificial feast (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.13">1Sa 9:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.5">16:5</reference>). Nebuchadnezzar was bidden to come to take vengeance on guilty Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.9">Jr 25:9</reference>). <div eID="gen24194" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fb50f554f2b6d724c319b8998534739db8b1cb6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12929"/><div sID="gen24195" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12929"/><hi type="bold">8. the princes--</hi>who ought to have been an example of good to others, but were ringleaders in all evil.<div eID="gen24195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24196" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the king's children--</hi>fulfilled on Zedekiah's children (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.6">Jr 39:6</reference>); and previously, on Jehoahaz and Eliakim, the sons of Josiah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.31">2Ki 23:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.36">36</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.6">2Ch 36:6</reference>; compare also <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.18">2Ki 20:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.13">21:13</reference>). Huldah the prophetess (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.20">2Ki 22:20</reference>) intimated that which Zephaniah now more expressly foretells.<div eID="gen24196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24197" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all such as are clothed with strange apparel--</hi>the princes or courtiers who attired themselves in costly garments, imported from abroad; partly for the sake of luxury, and partly to ingratiate themselves with foreign great nations whose costume as well as their idolatries they imitated, [Calvin]; whereas in costume, as in other respects, God would have them to be separate from the nations. Grotius refers the "strange apparel" to garments forbidden by the law, for example, men's garments worn by women, and vice versa, a heathen usage in the worship of Mars and Venus (<reference osisRef="Deut.22.5">De 22:5</reference>). <div eID="gen24197" type="x-p"/>
entries.44413d4ffa9584af0a8e8ab8975a60db40aa00cb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12930"/><div sID="gen24198" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12930"/><hi type="bold">9. those that leap on the threshold--</hi>the servants of the princes, who, after having gotten prey (like hounds) for their masters, leap exultingly on their masters' thresholds; or, on the thresholds of the houses which they break into [Calvin]. Jerome explains it of those who walk up the steps into the sanctuary with haughtiness. Rosenmuller translates, "Leap over the threshold"; namely, in imitation of the Philistine custom of not treading on the threshold, which arose from the head and hands of Dragon being broken off on the threshold before the ark (<reference osisRef="1Sam.5.5">1Sa 5:5</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.2.6">Is 2:6</reference>, "thy people ... are soothsayers like the Philistines." Calvin's view agrees best with the latter clause of the verse.<div eID="gen24198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24199" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fill ... masters' houses with violence, &c.--</hi>that is, with goods obtained with violence, &c. <div eID="gen24199" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7047f4f79f9a62a97cee134f0fccc2e8aefc4d5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12931"/><div sID="gen24200" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12931"/><hi type="bold">10. fish gate--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Chr.33.14">2Ch 33:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.3.3">Ne 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.12.39">12:39</reference>). Situated on the east of the lower city, north of the sheep gate [Maurer]: near the stronghold of David in Milo, between Zion and the lower city, towards the west [Jerome]. This verse describes the state of the city when it was besieged by Nebuchadnezzar. It was through the fish gate that he entered the city. It received its name from the fish market which was near it. Through it passed those who used to bring fish from the lake of Tiberias and Jordan. It answers to what is now called the Damascus gate [Henderson].<div eID="gen24200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24201" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the second--</hi>namely, the gate which was second in dignity [Calvin]. Or, the second or lower part of the city. Appropriately, the fish gate, or extreme end of the lower part of the city, first resounds with the cries of the citizens as the foe approaches; then, as he advances further, that part of the city itself, namely, its inner part; lastly, when the foe is actually come and has burst in, the hills, the higher ones, especially Zion and Moriah, on which the upper city and temple were founded [Maurer]. The second, or lower city, answers to Akra, north of Zion, and separated from it by the valley of Tyropoeon running down to the pool of Siloam [Henderson]. The Hebrew is translated "college," <reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.14">2Ki 22:14</reference>; so Vatablus would translate here.<div eID="gen24201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24202" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hills--</hi>not here those outside, but those within the walls: Zion, Moriah, and Ophel. <div eID="gen24202" type="x-p"/>
entries.1dae4b194e2e0d13a143b08422de303802b58aa6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12932"/><div sID="gen24203" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12932"/><hi type="bold">11. Maktesh--</hi>rather, "the mortar," a name applied to the valley of Siloam from its hollow shape [Jerome]. The valley between Zion and Mount Olivet, at the eastern extremity of Mount Moriah, where the merchants dwelt. <reference osisRef="Zech.14.21">Zec 14:21</reference>, "The Canaanite," namely, merchant [Chaldee Version]. The Tyropoeon (that is, cheese-makers') valley below Mount Akra [Rosenmuller]. Better Jerusalem itself, so called as lying in the midst of hills (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.1">Is 22:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.21.13">Jr 21:13</reference>) and as doomed to be the scene of its people being destroyed as corn or drugs are pounded in a mortar (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.22">Pr 27:22</reference>) [Maurer]. Compare the similar image of a "pot" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.3">Eze 24:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.6">6</reference>). The reason for the destruction is subjoined, namely, its merchant people's greediness of gain.<div eID="gen24203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all the merchant people--</hi>literally, the "Canaanite people": irony: all the merchant people of Jerusalem are very Canaanites in greed for gain and in idolatries (see on <reference osisRef="Hos.12.7">Ho 12:7</reference>).<div eID="gen24204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24205" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... that bear silver--</hi>loading themselves with that which will prove but a burden (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.6">Ha 2:6</reference>). <div eID="gen24205" type="x-p"/>
entries.684e559bf6583abaad60a588d44bc8aabd46011b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12933"/><div sID="gen24206" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12933"/><hi type="bold">12. search ... with candles--</hi>or lamps; so as to leave no dark corner in it wherein sin can escape the punishment, of which the Chaldeans are My instruments (compare <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.13">Zep 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.15.8">Lu 15:8</reference>).<div eID="gen24206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24207" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">settled on their lees--</hi>"hardened" or crusted; image from the crust formed at the bottom of wines long left undisturbed (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.11">Jr 48:11</reference>). The effect of wealthy undisturbed ease ("lees") on the ungodly is hardening: they become stupidly secure (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.55.19">Psa 55:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Am 6:1</reference>).<div eID="gen24207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24208" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord will not do good ... evil--</hi>They deny that God regards human affairs, or renders good to the good; or evil to the evil, but that all things go haphazard (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.4">Psa 10:4</reference>; Mal 2:17). <div eID="gen24208" type="x-p"/>
entries.2992f919b2f800d6f3edd223c3455383b249dd0c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12934"/><div sID="gen24209" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12934"/><hi type="bold">13. Therefore their goods shall become a booty, &c.--</hi>Fulfilling the prophecy in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.30">De 28:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.39">39</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.5.11">Am 5:11</reference>). <div eID="gen24209" type="x-p"/>
entries.783d30538ed2f791832b8f4d7c9f634f7d7c5391: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12935"/><div sID="gen24210" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12935"/><hi type="bold">14. voice of ... day of ... Lord--</hi>that is, Jehovah ushering in that day with a roar of vengeance against the guilty (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.30">Jr 25:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.2">Am 1:2</reference>). They who will not now heed (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.12">Zep 1:12</reference>) His voice by His prophets, must heed it when uttered by the avenging foe.<div eID="gen24210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24211" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mighty ... shall cry ... bitterly--</hi>in hopeless despair; the might on which Jerusalem now prides itself, shall then fail utterly. <div eID="gen24211" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5ecb6d08513e13aff071c7dea4e065ba17bf2aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12936"/><div sID="gen24212" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12936"/><hi type="bold">15. wasteness ... desolation--</hi>The Hebrew terms by their similarity of sounds, Shoah, Umeshoah, express the dreary monotony of desolation (see on <reference osisRef="Nah.2.10">Na 2:10</reference>). <div eID="gen24212" type="x-p"/>
entries.842876408566747799e81d314ef2f174e9e4225b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12937"/><div sID="gen24213" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12937"/><hi type="bold">16. the trumpet--</hi>namely, of the besieging enemy (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.2">Am 2:2</reference>).<div eID="gen24213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24214" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">alarm--</hi>the war shout [Maurer].<div eID="gen24214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">towers--</hi>literally, "angles"; for city walls used not to be built in a direct line, but with sinuous curves and angles, so that besiegers advancing might be assailed not only in front, but on both sides, caught as it were in a cul-de-sac; towers were built especially at the angles. So Tacitus describes the walls of Jerusalem [Histories, 5.11.7]. <div eID="gen24215" type="x-p"/>
entries.23003442584f5cbce856aef1486ab3e58e886ab9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12938"/><div sID="gen24216" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12938"/><hi type="bold">17. like blind men--</hi>unable to see whither to turn themselves so as to find an escape from existing evils.<div eID="gen24216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24217" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flesh--</hi>Hebrew, "bread"; so the Arabic term for "bread" is used for "flesh" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.26">Mt 26:26</reference>). <div eID="gen24217" type="x-p"/>
entries.d2402ecfcca4dad647cf07ef8ab65c8571a60b92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12939"/><div sID="gen24218" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12939"/><hi type="bold">18. Neither ... silver nor ... gold shall ... deliver them, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.11.4">Pr 11:4</reference>).<div eID="gen24218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24219" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fire of his jealousy--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.38.19">Eze 38:19</reference>); His wrath jealous for His honor consuming the guilty like fire.<div eID="gen24219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24220" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make even a speedy riddance of all--</hi>rather, a "consummation" (complete destruction: "full end," <reference osisRef="Jer.46.28">Jr 46:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.13">Eze 11:13</reference>) "altogether sudden" [Maurer]. "A consumption, and that a sudden one" [Calvin]. <chapter eID="Zeph.1"/>

entries.7ed9e2f7bda3f82e6b8bf1b2fbc631d268060aa6: <div eID="gen35233" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen35234" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35235" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35235" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35234" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35236" type="x-p"/> This chapter begins with denouncing God's judgments against Judah and Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Zep.1.1-Zep.1.3">Zep 1:1-3</reference>. Idolaters, and sinners of several other denominations, are then particularly threatened; and their approaching visitation enlarged on, by the enumeration of several circumstances which tend greatly to heighten its terrors, <reference osisRef="Zep.1.4-Zep.1.18">Zep 1:4-18</reference>. <div eID="gen35236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35237" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen35237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35238" type="x-p"/> The word of the Lord which came unto Zephaniah - Though this prophet has given us so large a list of his ancestors, yet little concerning him is known, because we know nothing certain relative to the persons of the family whose names are here introduced. We have one chronological note which is of more value for the correct understanding of his prophecy than the other could have been, how circumstantially soever it had been delivered; viz., that he prophesied in the days of Josiah, son of Amon, king of Judah; and from the description which he gives of the disorders which prevailed in Judea in his time, it is evident that he must have prophesied before the reformation made by Josiah, which was in the eighteenth year of his reign. And as he predicts the destruction of Nineveh, <reference osisRef="Zep.2.13">Zep 2:13</reference>, which, as Calmet remarks, could not have taken place before the sixteenth of Josiah, allowing with Berosus twenty-one years for the reign of Nabopolassar over the Chaldeans; we must, therefore, place this prophecy about the beginning of the reign of Josiah, or from b.c. 640 to b.c. 609. But see the chronological notes.
entries.40b8ced889304bf779fd11cc7a270b61e0ff8a44: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen35238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35239" type="x-p"/> I will utterly consume all things - All being now ripe for destruction, I will shortly bring a universal scourge upon the land. He speaks particularly of the idolaters.
entries.73f4ab92e24e762fc66a5977d01457c3c7700c31: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen35239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35240" type="x-p"/> I will consume man and beast - By war, and by pestilence. Even the waters shall he infected, and the fish destroyed; the air become contaminated, and the fowls die.
entries.d082ec526cd1150bf2e0679a9652f77cd6ea89b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen35240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35241" type="x-p"/> I will cut off the remnant of Baal - I think he refers here, partly at least, to the reformation which Josiah was to bring about. See the account, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.5">2Kgs 23:5</reference> (note). <div eID="gen35241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35242" type="x-p"/> The Chemarims - The black-robed priests of different idols. See the note on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.6">2Kgs 23:6</reference>. These were put down by Josiah.
entries.e8c806960e6aa7ca0fd691d9018a96d0f0541a08: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen35242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35243" type="x-p"/> The host of heaven - Sun, moon, planets, and stars. This worship was one of the most ancient and the most common of all species of idolatry; and it had a greater semblance of reason to recommend it. See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.6">2Kgs 23:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.12">2Kgs 23:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.19.13">Jer 19:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.29">Jer 32:29</reference>. <div eID="gen35243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35244" type="x-p"/> That swear by the Lord, and that swear by Malcham - Associating the name of an idol with that of the Most High. For Malcham, see on <reference osisRef="Hos.4.15">Hos 4:15</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Amo.5.26">Amo 5:26</reference> (note).
entries.f6a3dad33537615a26458f75e7216c16f3207f64: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen35244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35245" type="x-p"/> Them that are turned back - Who have forsaken the true God, and become idolaters. <div eID="gen35245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35246" type="x-p"/> Nor inquired for him - Have not desired to know his will.
entries.b293951d698b31173cf3ca5700d15a6718c65009: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen35246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35247" type="x-p"/> Hold thy peace at the presence of the Lords God - הס has, the same as hush, hist, among us. Remonstrances are now useless. You had time to acquaint yourselves with God; you would not: you cry now in vain; destruction is at the door. <div eID="gen35247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35248" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath prepared a sacrifice - A slaughter of the people. <div eID="gen35248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35249" type="x-p"/> He hath bid his guests - The Babylonians, to whom he has given a commission to destroy you. In all festivals sacrifices, <div eID="gen35249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35250" type="x-p"/> 1. The victims were offered to God, and their blood poured out before the altar. <div eID="gen35250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35251" type="x-p"/> 2. The people who were invited feasted upon the sacrifice. See on <reference osisRef="Isa.34.6">Isa 34:6</reference> (note).
entries.ac17a0fc0efdedfe34f68b15e998f95f666a753e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen35251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35252" type="x-p"/> I will punish the princes, and the king's children - After the death of Josiah the kingdom of Judah saw no prosperity, and every reign terminated miserably; until at last King Zedekiah and the king's children were cruelly massacred at Riblah, when Nebuchadnezzar had taken Jerusalem. <div eID="gen35252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35253" type="x-p"/> Strange apparel - I really think this refers more to their embracing idolatrous customs and heathen usages, than to their changing their dress. They acquired new habits, as we would say; customs, that they used as they did their clothing - at all times, and in every thing.
entries.804e1b78be73291e333e4d930b4565933b6d69b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen35253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35254" type="x-p"/> That leap on the threshold - Or, that leap over the threshold. It is most probable that the Philistines are here meant. After the time that Dagon fell before the ark, and his hands were broken off on the threshold of his temple, his worshippers would no more set a foot upon the threshold, but stepped or leaped over it, when they entered into his temple. The Chaldee understands this of the Philistines, without giving this reason for it. Some understand it of haughtiness and pride: others think that leaping on the threshold refers to the customs of the Arabs, who used to ride into people's houses and take away whatever they could carry; and that this is the reason why, in several parts of the East, they have their doors made very low, to prevent those depredators from entering. In this manner, we learn the Persians have frequently oppressed the poor Armenians, going on horseback into their houses, and taking whatever they thought proper. Mr. Harmer understands it in this way.
entries.00cff6ef14b186fc53c8e25946f199e9b88b507c: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen35254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35255" type="x-p"/> A cry from the fish-gate - This gate, which is mentioned <reference osisRef="Neh.3.3">Neh 3:3</reference>, was opposite to Joppa; and perhaps the way in which the news came of the irruption of the Chaldean army, the great crashing from the hills. <div eID="gen35255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35256" type="x-p"/> The second - Or second city, may here mean a part of Jerusalem, mentioned <reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.14">2Kgs 22:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.22">2Chr 34:22</reference>.
entries.de9bb58d2ecad175c6aa587d34b4d543cf92936d: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen35256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35257" type="x-p"/> Maktesh - Calmet says this signifies a mortar, or a rock in form of a mortar, and was the name of a quarter of Jerusalem where they hulled rice, corn, etc., according to St. Jerome. Some think the city of Jerusalem is meant, where the inhabitants should be beat and pounded to death as grain is pounded in a mortar. <div eID="gen35257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35258" type="x-p"/> Newcome translates it, the lower city, and considers it the valley in Jerusalem, which divided the upper from the lower city. <div eID="gen35258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35259" type="x-p"/> They that bear silver - The merchants, moneychangers, usurers, rich men.
entries.960509bd522fabeb8a41949a5723553de2e2e657: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen35259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35260" type="x-p"/> I will search Jerusalem with candles - I will make a universal and thorough search. <div eID="gen35260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35261" type="x-p"/> That are settled on their lees - Those who are careless, satisfied with the goods of this life; who trust in their riches, and are completely irreligious; who, while they acknowledge that there is a God, think, like the Aristotelians, that he is so supremely happy in the contemplation of his own excellences, that he feels it beneath his dignity to concern himself with the affairs of mortals.
entries.a7b02d3ec567dec271fb745b31c107c2e220c60e: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen35261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35262" type="x-p"/> Their goods (in which they trust) shall become a booty - To the Chaldeans. They shall have no profit of all their labors. The houses they have built they shall not inhabit; of the wine of the vineyards they have planted, they shall not drink. See <reference osisRef="Amo.5.11">Amo 5:11</reference>, where we find the same evils threatened.
entries.482762f53ec6e23d7594a2012280f62cb4bb8e1d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen35262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35263" type="x-p"/> The great day of the Lord is near - It commenced with the death of the good king Josiah, who was slain by Pharaoh-necho at Megiddo, and continued to the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar.
entries.490eb26d6bc1aeedcad04703abe3700967f0f62c: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen35263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35264" type="x-p"/> That day is a day of wrath - See <reference osisRef="Isa.22.5">Isa 22:5</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Jer.30.7">Jer 30:7</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Joe.2.2">Joe 2:2</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Joe.2.11">Joe 2:11</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Amo.5.18">Amo 5:18</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Zep.1.18">Zep 1:18</reference> (note), and the notes there. From the fourteenth to the sixteenth verse inclusive there is a most beautiful amplification of the disasters that were coming on Jerusalem; the invasion, incursion, attack, carnage, confusion, horrible din occasioned by the sound of the trumpet, the cries of the people, and the shrieks and groans of the dying, are pointed out with great force and mighty effect.
entries.510d99c03c815009e7be476a0d4be55d092e1077: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen35264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35265" type="x-p"/> They shall walk like blind men - Be in the most perplexing doubt and uncertainty; and while in this state, have their blood poured out by the sword of their enemies, and their flesh trodden under foot.
entries.28fde74bacd9c5baa6bdcc5708108ea7098b2bb3: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen35265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35266" type="x-p"/> Their silver nor their gold - In which they trusted, and from which they expected happiness; these shall not profit them in this awful day. And God will bring this about speedily; and a speedy riddance - a universal desolation, shall in a short time take place in every part of the land.  <chapter eID="Zeph.1"/> <div eID="gen35266" type="x-p"/>

entries.4206b05f4d8f38ba3db9e459412426fa308ef493: <div eID="gen16698" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-ms">Zephaniah</title> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16699" type="x-p"/> Person of the Prophet. - <hi type="italic">Zephaniah's</hi> family is traced back in the heading to his book through four members, namely, to his great-great-grandfather <hi type="italic">Hezekiah</hi>; from which it has been justly inferred, that inasmuch as the father only is mentioned as a general rule, Hezekiah must have been a celebrated man, and that in all probability the king of that name is intended. For the only other person of such a name mentioned in the earlier history is an Ephraimite called <hi type="italic">Yehizkiyâh</hi> in <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.12">2Ch 28:12</reference>, and he can hardly be the person intended. The circumstance that Hezekiah is not described as the king of that name by the predicate <hi type="italic">hammelekh</hi> or <hi type="italic">melekh Yehūdâh</hi>, furnishes no decided argument against this assumption, but may probably be explained on the ground that the predicate “king of Judah” follows immediately afterwards in connection with Josiah’s name. There is still less force in the objection, that in the genealogy of the kings only two generations occur between Hezekiah and Josiah, inasmuch as Manasseh reigned for fifty-five years, that is to say, for nearly two generations. The name Zephaniah (<hi type="italic">Tsephanyâh</hi>), i.e., he whom Jehovah hides or shelters, not <hi type="italic">“speculator et arcanorum Dei cognitor,”</hi> as Jerome explains it according to an erroneous derivation from <hi type="italic">tsâphâh</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">tsâphân</hi>, occurs again as the name of a priest (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jer 21:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.25">Jer 29:25</reference>, etc.), as well as of other persons (cf. Zec 6:10, Zec 6:14; <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.21">1Ch 6:21</reference>). The lxx write it Σοφονίας, <hi type="italic">Sophonias</hi>, according to their usual custom of expressing צ by σ, and the Sheva by a short vowel which is regulated by the full vowel that follows; they have also changed the <hi type="italic">a</hi> into <hi type="italic">o</hi>, as in the case of Γοδολίου for <hi type="italic">Gedalyâh</hi> in Zep 1:1. Nothing further is known concerning the prophet’s life. The statement in Ps. Doroth. and Ps. Epiph., that he sprang “from the tribe of Simeon, from the mountain of Sarabathá” (<hi type="italic">al.</hi> Baratha or Sabartharam), is quite worthless. The date at which he lived is determined by the statement in the heading to his book, to the effect that he prophesied under king Josiah the son of Amos, who reigned from 641 to 610 b.c. This agrees both with the place assigned to his book in the series of the minor prophets, namely, between Habakkuk and Haggai, and also by the contents of his prophecies. According to Zep 2:13., where he predicts the destruction of the kingdom of Asshur and the city of Nineveh, the Assyrian empire was still in existence in his time, and Nineveh was not yet conquered, which took place, according to our discussions on Nahum (pp. 380ff.), at the earliest, in the closing years of Josiah’s reign, and possibly not till after his death. Moreover, his description of the moral depravity which prevailed in Jerusalem coincided in many respects with that of Jeremiah, whose labours as a prophet commenced in the thirteenth year of Josiah. Along with the worship of Jehovah (Zep 1:5; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.6.20">Jer 6:20</reference>), he speaks of idolatry (Zep 1:4-5; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.7.17-Jer.7.18">Jer 7:17-18</reference>), of false swearing by Jehovah, and swearing by the idols (<hi type="italic">Zep 1:5</hi>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.2">Jer 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.9">Jer 7:9</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.5.7">Jer 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.12.16">Jer 12:16</reference>), of the wicked treatment of the <hi type="italic">thorâh</hi> (Zep 3:4; <reference osisRef="Jer.8.8-Jer.8.9">Jer 8:8-9</reference>), of the fruitlessness of all the admonitions that have hitherto been addressed to Judah (Zep 3:2; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.30">Jer 2:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.28">Jer 7:28</reference>), and of the deep moral corruption that has pervaded all ranks - the royal family, the princes, the prophets, and the priests (Zep 1:4, Zep 1:8-9; Zep 3:3-4; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.2.8">Jer 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.26">Jer 2:26</reference>).
